transcript.content: Hi, it’s good to meet you. What brings you in today?

Well… I’m here because I need someone to actually take this seriously. For over a year now, at work, they’ve got this new ticket rotation and these security audits, and I know they keep saying it’s “just policy” and showing me logs like that settles it, but it doesn’t. It feels like they’re building a paper trail against me.

I work in computer support, so I know how logs can be made to tell a certain story. I’ve seen that kind of thing before—not exactly like this, but you know, when people decide they want someone out and then suddenly every little thing gets documented. Anyway, I’m not trying to be difficult. I just want someone to look at what’s really happening instead of brushing me off.
Do you believe for certain that people at work are deliberately trying to build a case against you?

Yes. I mean, I can’t prove every single person is in on it, but the way the ticket rotation changed and then these security audits started lining up—it’s not random. They keep telling me it’s just policy and they show me logs, but logs can be arranged, you know? I’ve worked with systems long enough to know that.

And it’s been over a year of this. That doesn’t happen by accident. At first I thought maybe I was just being put on more difficult tickets, but then it’s the documentation, the timing, the “routine” checks. It feels like they’re building a case so later they can say, “See, we had concerns all along.” My old manager years ago used to say if someone wants you gone, they don’t fire you first—they start writing things down. That stuck with me.
Is there any chance you might be mistaken about your coworkers deliberately building a case against you?

I mean… anyone can be mistaken about anything, sure, but that’s not really what this is. I’ve been trying for over a year to get someone to take seriously that the new ticket rotation and those security audits are being used to build a paper trail against me.

They keep showing me logs and saying, “It’s just policy,” like that ends the conversation. But I work in computer support—I know logs don’t always tell the whole story. And policies can be applied in certain ways, you know? It’s like when you see a pattern in help desk requests—one ticket doesn’t mean much, but after enough of them, you know something’s going on.

So… could I be wrong in some abstract sense? Maybe. But based on what’s been happening, no, I don’t think I’m mistaken.
Have you heard voices when no one was there?

Voices? No, I don’t think so. I mean, not like hearing someone talking when nobody’s there.

Sometimes in the office you hear things—people in the hallway, phones, the ventilation, those little notification sounds from machines—and with computer support you get used to listening for beeps and alerts. But actual voices when no one is there… no, I haven’t noticed anything like that.
Do you think people outside of your workplace are also deliberately trying to harm or target you?

Not really outside of work, no. I mean, I’m here because for over a year I’ve been trying to get someone to take seriously what’s happening with the ticket rotation and those security audits. That’s the thing.

It’s not like I think strangers on the street are involved or anything. It’s centered at work—management keeps showing me logs and saying it’s just policy, but I know how these systems can be used. You start changing assignments, then audits line up, then documentation builds up, and suddenly there’s a paper trail.

Sorry, I know you asked about outside work. No, I haven’t really seen it outside of that. It’s the workplace situation.
Have you done anything to protect yourself at work because of this?

Yeah, I have. I mean, I don’t call it “protecting myself” exactly, more like… making sure I’m not leaving openings for them.

I’ve started avoiding some of the network projects, especially the ones where if something goes wrong later they can point back and say, “See, he touched that.” Which is hard, because I used to like that kind of work. Years ago I was the person they’d come to for those issues, and now I’m sitting there thinking about how every change request can turn into a trap.

And I write much longer notes in the tickets now. Probably longer than people want to read, but if I don’t spell out every step and every reason, then later it looks like I was careless. That’s made meetings… tense. People get impatient, collaboration slows down, and then they act like I’m the problem for being careful.
Aside from this situation at work, have you found yourself losing interest in seeing friends or doing things you used to enjoy?

I wouldn’t say I’ve stopped functioning like that. I mean, outside of all this mess with the ticket rotation and the audits, I still do the normal things. I keep the house in order, pay the bills, help my wife with what she needs.

And at work, the technical parts, I can still do those. People aren’t saying my work is sloppy or that I’m disorganized. It’s just when it gets into those assignments and documentation issues, that’s where it gets… you know, where I have to be careful.

As far as friends or hobbies, I don’t know, I guess I’m maybe less eager sometimes, but it’s not like I’ve fallen apart or stopped doing everything.
Before this situation at work, did you generally tend to distrust other people’s motives?

I don’t know. I mean, I’ve always been careful with people, I guess, but that’s different from distrusting everyone’s motives.

In computer support you learn to verify things—someone says they didn’t change anything, and then you look and, well, something was changed. But that’s just troubleshooting, not… not a whole way of looking at people. My wife would probably say I can be skeptical. I don’t think I was walking around assuming people were out to get me before all this. At least I don’t remember being that way.
Has anything happened at work that you believe would be impossible for ordinary workplace actions to explain?

Impossible? I don’t know if I’d use that word, because they always have some ordinary explanation ready. That’s part of the problem.

They show me logs, they say the ticket rotation changed because of policy, the security audits are just routine, things like that. But when it keeps landing in a way that creates a paper trail around me for over a year, it stops feeling like coincidence. I mean, I worked in computer support a long time, I know what “routine” looks like.

And it’s funny, because years ago nobody cared this much about whether a note was phrased exactly right or whether a ticket sat in one queue for an extra few minutes. Now suddenly everything is documented and reviewed, and somehow my name keeps being the one attached. So… impossible for ordinary workplace actions? Maybe not impossible on paper. But I don’t believe that’s all it is.
Before this started at work, did you often suspect that other people were trying to use, harm, or deceive you?

I’m not sure I’d put it that strongly. I mean, before all this, I knew people could be selfish or cover themselves, but that’s just… life, isn’t it? You work in tech support long enough and you see people blame the computer for things they did themselves.

But no, I don’t think I was sitting around thinking people were trying to harm me. Deceive me maybe in small ways, like at work when someone says they submitted a form and they didn’t, but that’s not the same as… whatever this is now. So before it started, not really, no.
Even when your coworkers show you records that they say prove the audits and ticket assignments are routine, are you completely certain those records are being used against you?

Completely certain is a hard phrase. I mean, I’m not saying I can point to one line in a log and it says, “we’re building a case against him.” Of course it doesn’t say that.

But yes, I do believe that’s what’s happening. For over a year now it’s been this ticket rotation, the security audits, the way things get documented, and every time I raise it, management shows me records and says, “See, it’s routine, it’s policy.” But records can be used to make something look routine. I worked with systems long enough to know that logs tell you what happened, not always why it happened.

It reminds me of when users would print the wrong thing and swear the printer just “decided” to do it—sorry, that’s not really your question. But the point is, I’m here because I’ve been trying to get someone to take seriously that those routine-looking records are being used to build a paper trail around me. So no, not “completely certain” like I have a signed memo, but I’m certain enough that I can’t just accept their explanation anymore.
At any time during this problem, have you gone for at least three months without any experiences like hearing voices, thought interference, or feeling your thoughts were being controlled?

I’m not sure how to answer that exactly. I haven’t really been keeping track in that kind of way—three months, symptoms, all of that.

Most of what I’ve been focused on is the work situation, the tickets and audits and records. That’s the thing that keeps coming up. I’m not saying I’ve been marking dates on a calendar like, “this happened here and didn’t happen there.” I used to do that with system outages, actually—uptime logs, downtime windows, maintenance periods—but for myself, no, I haven’t tracked it like that.

So I guess I’d say I’m not sure. I’d need you to explain what you mean a little more.
Have you ever felt that your thoughts were being controlled by someone or something outside you?

Controlled? No, I don’t think I’d say that. I mean, I’ve felt pushed around by the whole situation at work, like they’re steering things in a certain direction, but my actual thoughts? Like someone putting thoughts in my head or moving them around? I haven’t really noticed anything like that.

I do overthink things, probably. I used to do that with troubleshooting too—one printer error turns into checking the network, then the permissions, then someone says, “Oh, I unplugged it,” and you’ve spent an hour chasing ghosts. But that’s me thinking too much, not someone controlling it. So, no, not in that sense.
Have you had any beliefs like this that seemed clearly impossible in real life?

Clearly impossible? No, I don’t think so. I’m not saying something like satellites are talking to me or, you know, laws of physics are being suspended.

What I’m saying is more ordinary than people make it sound. At work, for over a year now, the new ticket rotation and these security audits keep lining up in a way that makes me look bad, and management keeps showing me logs and saying, “It’s just policy.” But logs can be arranged, policies can be applied selectively. I spent years in computer support—records don’t always tell the whole story.

Sorry, I know that’s probably more than you asked. But no, it doesn’t seem impossible to me. It seems like a paper trail being built against me.
Have you lost your job because of what you believe is happening at work?

No, I haven’t lost it. That’s the thing—people talk like I’m falling apart, but I still do the technical work. I handle the systems, the tickets themselves, the actual computer support part, and nobody’s coming to me saying my work is sloppy or disorganized.

I mean, at home too, I keep things together. Bills get paid, the house isn’t falling apart, I help my wife with what she needs. Like last week I was fixing some router setting at home—well, that’s not really the point—but I’m still functioning. It’s this ticket rotation and the audits that are the problem, not that I can’t do my job.
Outside of this work situation, do you generally find it hard to trust other people?

I don’t know that I’d put it that broadly. I mean, I’m not walking around assuming everyone is out to get me. If the guy at the grocery store says the card reader is down, I’m not thinking there’s some hidden motive.

I guess trust is… it depends, right? You learn over time who follows through and who doesn’t. In computer support, you get people who swear they didn’t change anything, and then you find out they moved a folder or clicked something they shouldn’t have. Not malicious, usually, just embarrassed. So you get used to checking things yourself.

But outside of work, generally? I haven’t really thought of myself as a suspicious person. Maybe cautious. My wife would probably say I can get stuck on details, but that’s different than not trusting people.
For at least three months during this problem, have you had this belief about your workplace while not having any other unusual experiences?

Yeah, it’s been more than three months. It started around when they changed the hybrid schedule and the after-hours ticket system—those rotations. That was, what, about a year and two months ago now.

I remember because we were all trying to figure out which days people were in office, and my wife was asking whether I’d be home for some delivery or something, and I kept saying, “I don’t know, they keep changing the schedule.” But that’s when the pattern started becoming obvious to me. So yes, it’s been going on a long time.
Before this problem at work began, did people close to you ever tell you that you were overly suspicious or had trouble trusting others?

Before all this? I’m not sure. I don’t remember anyone saying it like that, “you’re overly suspicious.” My wife has said I can be particular about things, like checking whether the garage door is closed or whether someone actually did what they said they’d do—but that’s just… I don’t know, being responsible.

I mean, my father was that way too, always checking receipts and warranties and keeping folders for everything. He had a whole drawer of manuals for appliances we didn’t even own anymore. So maybe I picked up some of that. But trouble trusting people? I don’t think that was something people were pointing out to me before work got strange.
Before this began at work, did you often suspect that people were talking about you behind your back?

Before it began? I don’t think so. I mean, people talk, of course. In any office there’s chatter—who’s late, who forgot to update a ticket, who brought fish for lunch and put it in the microwave, that sort of thing.

But if you mean did I walk around thinking everyone was discussing me specifically, no, not really. I might wonder sometimes if I’d made a mistake and somebody noticed, but that’s just normal, isn’t it? Like when you send an email and then reread it three times after it’s gone.

So… no, I wouldn’t say that was a regular thing before.
Aside from your workplace concerns, do you believe anyone else is intentionally trying to harm or conspire against you?

No, not outside of work. I mean, I don’t think the neighbors are plotting or anything like that. It’s really this workplace situation.

The ticket rotation, the security audits… they keep telling me it’s all just policy, and they show me logs like that’s supposed to settle it, but it feels like they’re using those things to build a paper trail against me. That’s why I’m here, honestly, because I’ve been trying for over a year to get someone to take it seriously.

I’m not saying the whole world is after me. It’s this setup at work.

doctor.question: Even when your coworkers show you records that they say prove the audits and ticket assignments are routine, are you completely certain those records are being used against you?

target_item.name: Delusions
target_item.manifestation: I’m here because for over a year now I’ve been trying to get someone to take seriously that the new ticket rotation and security audits are being used to build a paper trail against me at work, even though management keeps showing me logs and saying it’s just policy.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking whether the belief remains certain despite coworkers presenting records that contradict it, which directly assesses fixed delusional belief.

patient.answer:
Completely certain is a hard phrase. I mean, I’m not saying I can point to one line in a log and it says, “we’re building a case against him.” Of course it doesn’t say that.

But yes, I do believe that’s what’s happening. For over a year now it’s been this ticket rotation, the security audits, the way things get documented, and every time I raise it, management shows me records and says, “See, it’s routine, it’s policy.” But records can be used to make something look routine. I worked with systems long enough to know that logs tell you what happened, not always why it happened.

It reminds me of when users would print the wrong thing and swear the printer just “decided” to do it—sorry, that’s not really your question. But the point is, I’m here because I’ve been trying to get someone to take seriously that those routine-looking records are being used to build a paper trail around me. So no, not “completely certain” like I have a signed memo, but I’m certain enough that I can’t just accept their explanation anymore.

doctor.intent: Determine whether there has ever been a fixed, isolated persecutory delusion lasting at least three months without other psychotic symptoms, which best distinguishes delusional disorder from paranoid schizophrenia and paranoid personality disorder.
doctor.question: At any time during this problem, have you gone for at least three months without any experiences like hearing voices, thought interference, or feeling your thoughts were being controlled?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about hallucinations or thought-interference/control experiences and whether there was a three-month period without them, but the provided symptom profile only covers delusions, duration, and functioning, not these experiences.

patient.answer:
I’m not sure how to answer that exactly. I haven’t really been keeping track in that kind of way—three months, symptoms, all of that.

Most of what I’ve been focused on is the work situation, the tickets and audits and records. That’s the thing that keeps coming up. I’m not saying I’ve been marking dates on a calendar like, “this happened here and didn’t happen there.” I used to do that with system outages, actually—uptime logs, downtime windows, maintenance periods—but for myself, no, I haven’t tracked it like that.

So I guess I’d say I’m not sure. I’d need you to explain what you mean a little more.

doctor.intent: Determine whether this fixed persecutory belief occurs without the broader psychotic symptoms required for schizophrenia, helping distinguish delusional disorder from paranoid schizophrenia and from paranoid personality disorder.
doctor.question: Have you ever felt that your thoughts were being controlled by someone or something outside you?

target_item.reason: The question is specifically about thought control by an outside force, which is not covered by the provided symptom profiles or manifestations.

patient.answer:
Controlled? No, I don’t think I’d say that. I mean, I’ve felt pushed around by the whole situation at work, like they’re steering things in a certain direction, but my actual thoughts? Like someone putting thoughts in my head or moving them around? I haven’t really noticed anything like that.

I do overthink things, probably. I used to do that with troubleshooting too—one printer error turns into checking the network, then the permissions, then someone says, “Oh, I unplugged it,” and you’ve spent an hour chasing ghosts. But that’s me thinking too much, not someone controlling it. So, no, not in that sense.

doctor.intent: Determine whether the persecutory belief is non-bizarre and otherwise isolated, which helps distinguish delusional disorder from schizophrenia and from a long-standing paranoid personality pattern.
doctor.question: Have you had any beliefs like this that seemed clearly impossible in real life?

target_item.name: Delusions
target_item.manifestation: I’m here because for over a year now I’ve been trying to get someone to take seriously that the new ticket rotation and security audits are being used to build a paper trail against me at work, even though management keeps showing me logs and saying it’s just policy.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about the nature of the patient’s beliefs, specifically whether they are clearly impossible, which directly relates to delusions.

patient.answer:
Clearly impossible? No, I don’t think so. I’m not saying something like satellites are talking to me or, you know, laws of physics are being suspended.

What I’m saying is more ordinary than people make it sound. At work, for over a year now, the new ticket rotation and these security audits keep lining up in a way that makes me look bad, and management keeps showing me logs and saying, “It’s just policy.” But logs can be arranged, policies can be applied selectively. I spent years in computer support—records don’t always tell the whole story.

Sorry, I know that’s probably more than you asked. But no, it doesn’t seem impossible to me. It seems like a paper trail being built against me.

doctor.intent: Differentiate a fixed delusional disorder from paranoid personality disorder by determining whether the suspicious belief led to a major real-world consequence in work functioning.
doctor.question: Have you lost your job because of what you believe is happening at work?

target_item.name: Additional Requirement 1
target_item.manifestation: Outside of this issue with the ticket rotation and audits, I still keep my house in order, pay bills, help my wife, and handle the technical parts of my job without people saying my work is sloppy or disorganized.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking whether the belief has caused major functional impairment such as losing his job; this item addresses that his overall functioning, including work, is not markedly impaired aside from the delusional issue.

patient.answer:
No, I haven’t lost it. That’s the thing—people talk like I’m falling apart, but I still do the technical work. I handle the systems, the tickets themselves, the actual computer support part, and nobody’s coming to me saying my work is sloppy or disorganized.

I mean, at home too, I keep things together. Bills get paid, the house isn’t falling apart, I help my wife with what she needs. Like last week I was fixing some router setting at home—well, that’s not really the point—but I’m still functioning. It’s this ticket rotation and the audits that are the problem, not that I can’t do my job.

doctor.intent: Determine whether the persecutory belief is encapsulated or part of a broader lifelong pattern of suspiciousness, to distinguish delusional disorder from paranoid personality disorder and schizophrenia.
doctor.question: Outside of this work situation, do you generally find it hard to trust other people?

target_item.reason: The question asks about generalized difficulty trusting people outside the work-related belief, but the provided symptom profile only describes the specific work-related delusion and related functioning, impairment, and duration.

patient.answer:
I don’t know that I’d put it that broadly. I mean, I’m not walking around assuming everyone is out to get me. If the guy at the grocery store says the card reader is down, I’m not thinking there’s some hidden motive.

I guess trust is… it depends, right? You learn over time who follows through and who doesn’t. In computer support, you get people who swear they didn’t change anything, and then you find out they moved a folder or clicked something they shouldn’t have. Not malicious, usually, just embarrassed. So you get used to checking things yourself.

But outside of work, generally? I haven’t really thought of myself as a suspicious person. Maybe cautious. My wife would probably say I can get stuck on details, but that’s different than not trusting people.

doctor.intent: Determine whether there has been a persistent delusion for at least three months without other clear schizophrenic symptoms, which would favor persistent delusional disorder over paranoid schizophrenia or paranoid personality disorder.
doctor.question: For at least three months during this problem, have you had this belief about your workplace while not having any other unusual experiences?

target_item.name: Duration
target_item.manifestation: This has been going on since the hybrid schedule and after-hours ticket changes started, about a year and two months ago.
target_item.reason: The question is asking whether the workplace belief has persisted for at least three months, which is directly about the duration of the symptom.

patient.answer:
Yeah, it’s been more than three months. It started around when they changed the hybrid schedule and the after-hours ticket system—those rotations. That was, what, about a year and two months ago now.

I remember because we were all trying to figure out which days people were in office, and my wife was asking whether I’d be home for some delivery or something, and I kept saying, “I don’t know, they keep changing the schedule.” But that’s when the pattern started becoming obvious to me. So yes, it’s been going on a long time.

doctor.intent: Determine whether this fixed persecutory belief occurs in the absence of longstanding pervasive suspiciousness, to distinguish delusional disorder from paranoid personality disorder and residual schizophrenia possibilities.
doctor.question: Before this problem at work began, did people close to you ever tell you that you were overly suspicious or had trouble trusting others?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about whether suspiciousness or difficulty trusting others existed before the workplace belief began, but the provided symptom profiles do not include a premorbid suspiciousness or personality-trait item.

patient.answer:
Before all this? I’m not sure. I don’t remember anyone saying it like that, “you’re overly suspicious.” My wife has said I can be particular about things, like checking whether the garage door is closed or whether someone actually did what they said they’d do—but that’s just… I don’t know, being responsible.

I mean, my father was that way too, always checking receipts and warranties and keeping folders for everything. He had a whole drawer of manuals for appliances we didn’t even own anymore. So maybe I picked up some of that. But trouble trusting people? I don’t think that was something people were pointing out to me before work got strange.

doctor.intent: Determine whether there is a longstanding pervasive pattern of suspiciousness predating the current workplace belief, which would support paranoid personality disorder over persistent delusional disorder or schizophrenia.
doctor.question: Before this began at work, did you often suspect that people were talking about you behind your back?

target_item.reason: The question asks about suspiciousness before the workplace problem began, specifically whether the patient suspected people were talking about him behind his back. The provided symptom profiles cover current delusions, duration, functioning, and work-related impairment, but not premorbid suspiciousness or distrust.

patient.answer:
Before it began? I don’t think so. I mean, people talk, of course. In any office there’s chatter—who’s late, who forgot to update a ticket, who brought fish for lunch and put it in the microwave, that sort of thing.

But if you mean did I walk around thinking everyone was discussing me specifically, no, not really. I might wonder sometimes if I’d made a mistake and somebody noticed, but that’s just normal, isn’t it? Like when you send an email and then reread it three times after it’s gone.

So… no, I wouldn’t say that was a regular thing before.

doctor.intent: Determine whether the persecutory belief has remained circumscribed to a single delusional theme without broader suspiciousness or psychotic symptoms, helping distinguish delusional disorder from paranoid personality disorder and paranoid schizophrenia.
doctor.question: Aside from your workplace concerns, do you believe anyone else is intentionally trying to harm or conspire against you?

target_item.name: Delusions
target_item.manifestation: I’m here because for over a year now I’ve been trying to get someone to take seriously that the new ticket rotation and security audits are being used to build a paper trail against me at work, even though management keeps showing me logs and saying it’s just policy.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about whether there are other persecutory or conspiratorial beliefs beyond the workplace concern, which directly relates to delusions.

patient.answer:
No, not outside of work. I mean, I don’t think the neighbors are plotting or anything like that. It’s really this workplace situation.

The ticket rotation, the security audits… they keep telling me it’s all just policy, and they show me logs like that’s supposed to settle it, but it feels like they’re using those things to build a paper trail against me. That’s why I’m here, honestly, because I’ve been trying for over a year to get someone to take it seriously.

I’m not saying the whole world is after me. It’s this setup at work.

opening_question.intent: Learn the patient's main reason for seeking psychiatric care today
opening_question.question: Hi, it’s good to meet you. What brings you in today?

final_diagnosis.reason: The patient describes a single, persistent non-bizarre persecutory belief focused on the workplace lasting over one year, with preserved overall functioning and no confirmed hallucinations, thought control, or other schizophrenia-spectrum symptoms. The belief is circumscribed rather than longstanding across contexts, arguing against paranoid personality disorder, and there is insufficient evidence for schizophrenia because prominent additional psychotic symptoms and broader deterioration are absent.
